questions.t: A cyclist rides 30 km from Alton to Bexley. She rides <var>d</var> km of the trip at 40 km/h and the remainder at 60 km/h.
p: How far does she ride at 60 km/h, in terms of <var>d</var>?

Write an expression for the total time of the journey.
Find the total time in minutes if (i) d = 12 km,  (ii) d = 30 km.
questions.a:
a) (30 − d) km b) (i) d40 h (ii) 30 − d60 h c) d40 + 30 − d60 h d) (i) 0.6 h = 36 min (ii) 0.75 h = 45 min
Marker's note: at d = 30 the whole trip is at 40 km/h — the second term vanishes. A student who still adds a 60 km/h leg has misread the model.

questions.t: Consider the five numbers  −9,  −5,  −2,  3,  7.
p: What is the least (most negative) product you can make by multiplying two of them?
What is the greatest product you can make by multiplying two of them?
What is the least product you can make by multiplying three of them?
questions.a:
a) −63 (−9 × 7) b) 45 (−9 × −5) c) −189 (−9 × 3 × 7)
Marker's note: (c) is the trap. The instinct is −9 × −5 × 7, but two negatives give +315 — the greatest, not the least. A least product needs an odd number of negative factors.

questions.t: Are the two terms like terms? Answer yes or no, and give a one-line reason.
questions.a:
a) No — ab and a are different variable parts b) Yes — y2x is the same as xy2 c) No — a2 and a differ d) Yes — nm = mn e) No — x2y and xy2 differ
Section note, from the marked originals — two separate faults. In 8ab − 5a + 3ab + 8a the ab and a terms were merged — they are not like terms; the answer is 11ab + 3a and stays as two terms. In 7xy − 11xy2 + 2x2 + 3y2x the pair 3y2x and −11xy2 are like terms, giving −8xy2. Rewriting every term in alphabetical order first makes both visible.

questions.t: Solve each equation. Here the whole numerator is divided.
questions.a: a) 3 − 2x = 10, x = −312 b) 5 − x = 12, x = −7 c) 4 − 3x = 16, x = −4

questions.t: Solve both of these, then explain in one sentence why the answers are different.
questions.a:
(i) x = 4 (ii) x = −2. In (i) only x is halved, so the 6 is untouched; in (ii) the whole of 6 − x is halved, so multiplying by 2 gives 6 − x = 8.
Section note, from the marked original — that question read 3 − 2x/5 = 2, which is ambiguous as written. Read with normal precedence it means 3 − (2x/5) = 2, giving x = 212. Read as (3 − 2x)/5 = 2 it gives x = −312. Both are correct answers to different questions. Writing fractions stacked, never with a slash, removes the ambiguity — which is why every fraction in this paper is set that way.

questions.t: Solve 5(x + 2) − x = 9 − 2(x − 1), then check your answer by substituting it into both sides separately.
questions.a:
4x + 10 = 11 − 2x, so 6x = 1 and x = 16. Check: both sides = 323.
Section note: in 9 − 2(x − 1) the expansion is −2x + 2, not −2x − 2 — the −2 multiplies the −1 inside the bracket. An unusual answer such as 16 is not itself a sign of error, which is why the check is worth 2 of the 4 marks.

questions.t: Use algebra. In each part, start by saying clearly what your pronumeral stands for.
p: Maya is 24 years older than her daughter Ava. In 4 years’ time Maya will be three times as old as Ava. Find both of their current ages.
Tom is 28 years older than his son Kai. In 8 years’ time Tom will be three times as old as Kai. Find both of their current ages.
Priya is 24 years older than her son Dev. In 3 years’ time Priya will be three times as old as Dev. Find both of their current ages.
questions.a:
a) a + 28 = 3(a + 4) → Ava 8, Maya 32 b) k + 36 = 3(k + 8) → Kai 6, Tom 34 c) d + 27 = 3(d + 3) → Dev 9, Priya 33
Section note: the usual failure is adding the years to only one of the two ages — both people age. Writing the future ages as a column of two before forming the equation prevents it.

questions.t: Use algebra.
p: The sum of two numbers is 84, and one of them is five times the other. Find the two numbers.
The sum of two numbers is 60, and one of them is 8 less than three times the other. Find the two numbers.
questions.a: a) x + 5x = 84 → 14 and 70 b) x + (3x − 8) = 60 → 17 and 43
